---
title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
jupyter: python3
---

In an SEIR model, people infected first pass through a latent period (E, exposed) before they become infectious. In the simplest SEIR, the time spent in each state is exponentially distributed: many people leave a state almost at once and a few stay a long time, which is rarely realistic. A gamma-distributed (Erlang) period with a few stages is closer to most real infections: each person passes through *k* stages, each exponential, and the total has the same mean but much less spread. This page compares the two, for the same mean infectious period.

## The model

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| β | 0.3 per day | Rate of infection per susceptible person, per unit of the share infectious |
| Latent period | 5 days | Mean time in E (exponential) |
| Infectious period | 10 days | Mean time in I: exponential, or Erlang with 3 stages |
| R0 | 3 | β × the mean infectious period |
| Population | 100,000 | |
| Infectious at the start | 0.1% | |

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

def make_seir(infectious_period):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection = S >> E @ 0.3*I
    latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(5)
    recovery  = I >> R @ infectious_period
    return ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='seir')

exponential = make_seir(ss.days(10))
erlang = make_seir(ss.erlang(mean=ss.days(10), k=3))
```

The infection leads to E, so the people infected at the start are put in I with `init=dict(I=0.001)`. The diagram, from `diagram()`:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fence = '`' * 3
print(fence + '{mermaid}\n' + erlang.diagram() + '\n' + fence)
```

As an ODE, the Erlang period is exact: I is split into three stages, each with a mean of a third of the period, as the equations show:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0)
sim.run()
erlang.equations()
```

## Result

```{python}
sims = {
    'Exponential': ss.Sim(exponential, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0),
    'Erlang, 3 stages': ss.Sim(erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('seir')
```

Both have the same R0, so the same share of people is infected in the end. But with the Erlang period, people infect others over a narrower window of time after they were infected, so the epidemic grows faster, and peaks earlier and higher. A model fitted to the growth of an epidemic with the wrong distribution of the infectious period gets R0 wrong, which is one reason for the stages.
